notes:
I ran out of research steps before I could open several key sources: the rest of Enduring Word (vv. 16–36), Precept Austin's full page, NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, and the Catholic and Orthodox sites. So the notes below are thin for vv. 10–18, 20 and 29–36. I found nothing at all on Orthodox readings or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

**Judges 1: research notes**

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): Israel has lost its next leader, and Joshua named no successor. Asking the LORD was the right thing to do; now they must trust God more directly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/
- Ellicott (Anglican): he argues that most of 1:1–2:5 probably happened *before* Joshua died. He lists suggested explanations and settles on the view that "after the death of Joshua" works as a heading for the whole book. He thinks "inquired of the LORD" means asking through the high priest using the Urim and Thummim. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary takes the opposite view. The opening words imply the events happened very shortly after Joshua's death, and apostasy should not be thought to have caused the renewed war, since Israel served the Lord through the elders' lifetime. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/judges-1.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: God chose Judah, the Messiah's tribe and also the largest and strongest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/
- Ellicott: "go up" is a military term. The question was which tribe fights first, not who leads. He links the choice to Jacob's blessing on Judah (Gen 49:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- Precept Austin: Judah won because they trusted and obeyed God's promise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_1_commentary

**v. 3**
- JFB: their territories bordered each other, so they shared an interest and naturally joined forces. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_001.cfm
- Ellicott: Simeon's land lay inside Judah's. Simeon had shrunk badly between the two wilderness censuses and would have been helpless alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- Guzik: a picture of the church working as one body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/
- Matthew Henry: Christians of different "tribes" should strengthen one another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-5.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: Bezek means "lightning." He identifies it with the Bezek of 1 Sam 11:8, in central Palestine, so the two tribes may first have struck at the heart of Canaanite power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- The location is disputed:
  - JFB puts Bezek about twelve miles south of Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_001.cfm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the site is unknown, probably different from 1 Sam 11:8's Bezek. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-5.htm
  - Precept Austin identifies it with Khirbet Ibziq, north of Tubass. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_1_commentary

**v. 5**
- Clarke: "found" means a hostile encounter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-1.html
- Ellicott: "Adoni-bezek" is a title meaning "lord of Bezek," not a personal name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- Keil & Delitzsch suggest he may have marched from the north, so Judah and Simeon had to deal with him before taking their own land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-5.htm
- *Modern critical view (Cambridge Bible, quoted on Bible Hub):* it is hard to resist concluding Adoni-bezek is the same person as Adoni-zedek of Joshua 10. Moore suggests the name may have been changed to give it a contemptuous twist. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-5.htm
- Coffman disagrees: he should not be confused with Adonizedek. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/1-1.html

**v. 6**
- Most commentators say the purpose was to disable him: no thumbs, so he could not hold a weapon; no big toes, so he could not run. Sources: Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-6.htm; Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/1-5.html
- Ellicott adds that either injury would cost him his throne. He sees the punishment as an "eye for eye" penalty that Moses allowed in order to limit blood feuds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- JFB: it would have been a foul stain on Israel's character if it weren't retributive justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-6.htm
- Geneva Study Bible: God's just judgment, as the tyrant himself confesses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: it may seem cruel, yet it was simply justice in its truest sense. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/
- Matthew Henry: God sometimes makes the punishment answer the sin. Worldly power is slippery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_001.cfm
- On "seventy kings":
  - Ellicott: any petty chief could be called "king." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch: a round number, certainly hyperbole. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-7.htm
- Clarke reads "under my table" as a proverbial expression for the meanest servitude. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-1.html
- On whether the king knew the true God:
  - Clarke thinks he had knowledge of the true God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-1.html
  - Ellicott thinks he only recognised divine retribution in general. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- **Real disagreement among evangelicals: was sparing him obedience or failure?** Precept Austin, drawing on GotQuestions, says bringing him to Jerusalem shows disobedience. He was allowed to live in direct disregard of God's command, and God did not specifically command the maiming. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_1_commentary Guzik, Henry and JFB (above) present it as just retribution and do not criticise it.
- Constable: Adoni-bezek's humbling happens in Jerusalem, just as the later humbling of the Judean monarchy will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-1.html
- *Catholic (Haydock):* Israel treated him as he had treated others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/1-5.html

**v. 8** (how it fits with v. 21)
- Guzik: Jerusalem was held for a while, then fell back to the Jebusites until David took it about 400 years later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/
- Matthew Henry: Judah took the city now, but defenders who retreated into the castle held out till David's time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/1-1.html
- Ellicott: the KJV's "had" ("had fought," "had taken") is an unwarranted addition. Either the Jebusites kept the citadel or they retook the city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html
- JFB, by contrast, treats the capture as an early event of the invasion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_001.cfm

**v. 9**
- Guzik, following Cundall, explains the three regions: hill country, Negev and Shephelah (the foothills). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/
- Ellicott: "went down" is the term for particular battles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-1.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Hebron is where the Anakim once frightened the spies (Num 13). It was given to Caleb. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/

**vv. 12–13**
- Guzik: Caleb, a brave man himself, encouraged courage in the next generation. His nephew Othniel later becomes a judge (Judg 3:9–11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/

**vv. 14–15**
- Guzik summarises Spurgeon's sermon "Achsah's Asking, A Pattern of Prayer." Its points:
  - Achsah knew what she wanted before she asked.
  - She asked for help in making her request.
  - She thanked her father for past gifts and used them as grounds to ask for more.
  - Spurgeon compares the "springs" to the continual blessing of the Holy Spirit.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-1/

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew seems purposely to avoid saying "could not." Judah could have driven them out; but their faith was cowed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-19.htm
- Gill (Baptist): iron chariots were no reason why they could not drive them out, if God was with them. They were only the reason Israel was afraid. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/judges/1-19.html
- Matthew Henry: Israel had God, whose chariots are thousands of angels (Ps 68:17), yet they suffered their fears to prevail against their faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-19.htm
- Clarke: were the iron chariots too strong for Omnipotence? The whole of this verse is improperly rendered. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/judges/1-19.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the chariots were genuinely formidable, and Israel had no means of coping with them. https://biblehub.com/judges/1-19.htm
- *Translations:*
  - The NET Bible renders it chariots with iron-rimmed wheels. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/judges/1-19.html
  - The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) has chariots armed with scythes. https://biblehub.com/judges/1-19.htm
  - The Greek Septuagint says Rechab prevented them. https://biblehub.com/judges/1-19.htm

**v. 21** — See v. 8.

**vv. 22–23**
- Guzik: "house of Joseph" is an unusual combined name for Ephraim and Manasseh. The real reason for victory was that the LORD was with them, not clever spying. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/judges/judges-1.cfm
- Barnes: Bethel lay in Benjamin's territory but was taken by Joseph. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-24.htm
- Ellicott: Luz may mean "hazel." https://biblehub.com/judges/1-23.htm

**vv. 24–26**
- Commentators mostly read "the entrance" as a weak point or hidden way into the city, not the main gate. Gill mentions a Jewish tradition of a cave entrance. Keil & Delitzsch compare the promise with the one made to Rahab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-24.htm
- JFB assumes the promise depended on the man embracing the true religion, or quitting the country, as he did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-24.htm
- Bible Hub's own study notes (modern evangelical) are more critical. Unlike Rahab, he seems unmoved toward Israel's God, and his new city is likened to Cain's. https://biblehub.com/judges/1-26.htm Another Bible Hub article warns that compassion without consecration soon becomes compromise. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Luz_important_in_Judges_1_26.htm

**v. 28** (also applies to vv. 27–35)
- One commentator quoted on Bible Hub (name not shown in the excerpt) says Israel broke the law: anyone strong enough to collect tribute could have driven them out. Israel chose forced labour out of sloth and covetousness. Gill agrees: it came from covetousness, and a love of ease. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-28.htm
- Matthew Henry on vv. 21–36: the failures came from laziness, cowardice and greed. He applies this to believers whose graces languish, his lusts revive when they stop fighting their sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/1-24.htm

**vv. 29–36** — Nothing specific to these verses beyond the general comments under v. 28.

**Where Protestant traditions differ**
I found no real split along denominational lines in this chapter. Gill (Baptist), Ellicott (Anglican), Matthew Henry, Clarke and Guzik all blame v. 19 on Israel's lack of faith, not on God. The actual disagreements are between individual commentators, not traditions:
- the date of the events in v. 1;
- whether Adoni-bezek is the same person as Adoni-zedek;
- whether sparing Adoni-bezek and the man of Luz showed obedience or failure.
